headlines.title: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses
headlines.summary: Amazon's $250 Ring Drone Cam flies from room to room to investigate suspicious activity, and can capture footage at night.
headlines.article_text: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone, robot to patrol homes, businesses Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Amazon's Ring unveiled a flying indoor security drone and a patrolling robot for businesses. The $250 Ring Drone Cam flies from room to room to investigate suspicious activity, and can capture footage at night. The $1,000 Ring Rover Cam repurposes Amazon's Astro robot for deployment in workplaces, such as warehouses and offices. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Amazon's Ring unveiled a flying indoor security camera that lets users autonomously check on their home. Ring Amazon 's Ring is going deeper into surveillance with an indoor drone for home monitoring and an autonomous robot designed to patrol businesses. The company on Tuesday unveiled the $250 Ring Drone Cam, a security camera that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, as well as capture footage during the day or at night. When an alarm or sensor on windows, doors and home security devices is triggered, the textbook-sized drone travels a preset path to investigate suspicious activity. Users can also deploy the drone at any time, the company said. At a demo in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff said the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime "deterrent" due to the device's built-in LED lights. "If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window," Siminoff said. "You're probably not going to go into that house." The drone, which can fly up to eight minutes at a time before autonomously returning to its charging dock, has two plastic-encased propellers that emit a loud buzz when it's airborne. Ring devices have provided Amazon another avenue to grow its presence in the smart home beyond its Echo smart speakers and Eero routers, expanding in a market that Grand View Research estimates will top $200 billion in sales this year. It's equally fertile ground for Amazon rivals Apple and Google . Ring, which Amazon acquired in 2018 and is known for its doorbells, has been beset with privacy concerns , primarily due to its partnerships with police. Earlier this year, Ring faced renewed scrutiny over a controversial Super Bowl ad touting an AI pet-finding tool called "Search Party." It then canceled an integration with police tech provider Flock Safety , which has also faced widespread backlash over its automated license plate readers. Ring repurposed Amazon's Astro consumer robot, first unveiled in 2021, to be a business security device. Ring Ring first previewed its drone, then called the Always Home Cam , in 2020. Siminoff said he chose to hold off on releasing the device until Amazon could perfect the design, sensors and data processing. The company on Tuesday also debuted the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam. The device repurposes Amazon's Astro home robot , which had a short life as a business device and has seen few upgrades since its 2021 debut, for companies to use to patrol offices, warehouses and other workspaces. Ring said it "leveraged the best of Astro" to build the Ring Rover Cam, which it describes as a "purpose-built security robot." Similar to the Astro, the device is a display mounted on a two-wheeled base with an extendable periscope camera. It also features a "built-in siren," two-way audio and a "light tower" that shines onto the ceiling to help users keep track of its whereabouts. Siminoff said in an interview that the drone and the robot allow users to monitor multiple areas of their home or business with just one device. "People like indoor cameras, but they don't necessarily want them everywhere around their home," Siminoff said. Ring said privacy is the "default" mode for both the drone and the robot, which flash an LED light when they're recording. Siminoff said the drone can't fly outside per Federal Aviation Administration regulations, which restrict operating drones unless they're within a line of sight of a pilot. "We have told our customers not to do that because it's illegal," Siminoff said. "We've also put guardrails in there to make it so it doesn't fly outside." The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said. headlines.article_text: Trump administration moves to cut food stamps for 6.3 million people Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu A resident browses donated food items in the pantry at Feeding South Florida in Pembroke Park, Florida, US, on Friday, Oct. 31, 2025. About 42 million Americans could see their food assistance cut off within days as the US government shutdown stretches toward its second month, threatening to deepen economic pain and test Washington's resolve in one of the longest funding lapses in US history. Photographer: Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg via Getty Images Eva Marie Uzcategui | Bloomberg | Getty Images The Trump administration on Tuesday moved to cut millions more Americans from the nation's largest food assistance program, even as enrollment continues to fall from other administration cuts. A proposed rule issued by the U.S. Department of Agriculture would curb automatic eligibility for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, also known as food stamps, for households receiving cash aid under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families Program. Currently, households receiving TANF benefits qualify for SNAP without needing to meet federal income thresholds. TANF eligibility varies by state but is generally 130% to 200% of the federal poverty level. SNAP eligibility is generally 130% of the federal poverty level. Under the USDA's proposed change, nearly 18% of SNAP recipients, or about 6.3 million people, would lose benefits, according to an agency analysis included in the proposed rule. The changes would make SNAP eligibility more standardized and "preserve benefits for the truly needy," the rule said. More than 5.5 million people have already lost SNAP benefits since President Donald Trump enacted cuts to the program in his July 2025 tax law, bringing enrollment to about 36 million people, according to USDA data. The enrollment decline is partly due to struggles by states to implement administrative changes to the program and also to absorb significant new costs from Trump's law. Because SNAP enrollment also confers eligibility for other food aid programs, the USDA estimates that 1.8 million children would also lose eligibility for free school lunch under its proposed rule. Democratic Representative Angie Craig of Minnesota, ranking member of the House Agriculture Committee, in a statement called the rule "heartless and cruel." "The proposed rule would make it harder to meet basic needs and roll back efforts to streamline federal programs," she said. The public will have 30 days to comment on the proposed rule. David Ryder | Reuters Boeing said on Tuesday it delivered 49 jets in October, down from 57 the previous month and 53 a year earlier. However, Boeing had its strongest October for orders minus cancellations since 1997, booking 165 new orders with no cancellations. Most of those came from lessor Avolon's order for 140 737 MAX jets. Boeing delivered 32 737 MAX jets in October, down from 43 in September, with CEO Kelly Ortberg saying last month that it would miss its 737 delivery target of about 500 jets this year. Deliveries also included 11 787 Dreamliners, two 777 freighters and three 767s, including one for Boeing Defense's KC-46 tanker program. The lower deliveries come as Boeing works to raise 737 production to 47 jets a month, a rate Ortberg said the company would reach in early 2027. Wing production for 737 jets remains a constraint, and a supplier dispute has stalled wing production for 777 freighters and 767s. Through October, the US planemaker has delivered 524 jets, up about 6% from 493 a year earlier, well behind European rival Airbus , which delivered 621 in the first 10 months of the year. Air New Zealand took delivery of two 787s despite still waiting for certification by European regulators of its economy-class Skyrest sleep pods, according to the airline and news reports. Of the October orders, 150 were for 737 MAX jets: 140 for Avolon, six for Allegiant Air and four for unidentified customers. The other 15 were 787s for unidentified customers.
